Summary answer
Across collaborative mathematical argumentation, students’ processes shift from private conjecturing and individual verification toward shared claims, public warrants, and negotiated validation, supported by dialogic moves that externalize, elicit, and coordinate perspectives and by task designs that scaffold phases from exploration to critique and refinement. <cite id="c004a74e-0">Mathematically rich tasks promote discussion, multiple strategies, and justification, but the quality of collective argumentation depends strongly on group composition and teacher facilitation</cite>. <cite id="c004a74e-1">Collaborative knowledge construction distinguishes externalization, elicitation, and conflict resolution enacted through elaboration, agreement, and questioning</cite>, while <cite id="f6786a65-0">Toulmin-style coding captures how claims, data, warrants, qualifiers, and rebuttals coalesce into arguments during small-group work</cite>. <cite id="f82297c0-0">In modeling, groups progress through phases—model development (assumptions, variables), presentation (whole-group justification with social and ethical interpretation), and revision (hybrid mathematical-socio-critical critique)—with argumentation types shifting across phases</cite>, and <cite id="c004a74e-2">in proof work, group dialogue can yield complementary or reconstructive shifts, often moving reasoning from inductive to deductive structures</cite>.

How collaboration changes processes over time

1) From exploration to conjecturing: externalization and sense-making
Early collaboration is characterized by externalizing partial understandings and testing interpretations through dialogic moves that make tacit ideas explicit. <cite id="c004a74e-1">Externalization includes elaborating on others’ views, agreeing to keep threads alive, and answering posed questions to shape the flow of dialogue</cite>, enabling members to clarify different opinions and surface task-relevant knowledge. <cite id="c004a74e-0">Rich tasks prompt active engagement and multiple solution strategies, but group composition shapes whether students externalize and coordinate effectively</cite>. <cite id="c004a74e-0">Heterogeneous groups often see higher-ability peers supporting less able members, improving discussion quality and shared understanding, whereas homogeneous groups can converge more quickly but risk uniformity; low-ability groups struggle with setting tasks and critiquing data</cite>. <cite id="f6786a65-0">As students talk, claims and data emerge, with warrants still implicit; Toulmin components can be identified in short bursts, and a minimum Data–Claim pairing is required for an argument to count</cite>. <cite id="f82297c0-0">In modeling’s Phase 1, groups define the problem, make assumptions, and identify variables, with collective argumentation dominated by mathematical arguments focused on model construction</cite>.

2) From private warrants to public justification: structuring arguments and warrants
As groups move to justify interim claims, discourse becomes more structured: students articulate data, connect evidence to conclusions via warrants, and qualify confidence. <cite id="f6786a65-1">Students build arguments by employing evidence and warrants to support claims, with wagers serving as reasonable justifications such as axioms or theorems</cite>. <cite id="f6786a65-2">Collective argumentation integrates social and cognitive perspectives: students both construct and evaluate arguments by examining the warrant linking evidence to claim</cite>. <cite id="f6786a65-0">Rebuttals and qualifiers become common, and the Data–Claim–Warrant core crystallizes into arguments that can be documented across a small-group session</cite>. <cite id="f82297c0-1">Across phases, three argumentation types can be distinguished—mathematical, socio-critical, and hybrid—with mathematical argumentation predominating during model development as groups focus on formulating and justifying claims</cite>.

3) From agreement-seeking to critical evaluation: critique, counterexamples, and hybridization
As public justification surfaces tensions, groups increasingly engage in critique, challenge assumptions, and integrate divergent perspectives. <cite id="c004a74e-1">Requesting task- or strategy-related information and questioning mathematics supports abstraction and deepens knowledge use</cite>, while <cite id="c004a74e-0">teachers’ facilitation is crucial to sustain productive critique and orchestrate collective argumentation</cite>. <cite id="f82297c0-2">In Phase 2, whole-group presentations trigger socio-critical argumentation about contextual appropriateness and ethical implications; returning to small groups in Phase 3, students adopt a hybrid mode that integrates mathematical precision with socio-critical insight</cite>. <cite id="f6786a65-0">Rebuttals function as objections specifying conditions under which claims fail, and backing and qualifiers modulate strength of claims</cite>. <cite id="f82297c0-0">This shift toward hybrid argumentation during revision reflects coordinated efforts to check assumptions, verify procedures, and refine solutions</cite>.

4) From individual to collective reasoning structures: induction to deduction, complementarity to reconstruction
Group work can transform individual reasoning into collective reasoning structures and stances. <cite id="c004a74e-2">When undergraduates moved from individual to group work on a proof task, four students exhibited complementary shifts—reconsidering and extending their initial structures—while five underwent reconstructive shifts, entirely revising prior views; in all cases, reasoning shifted from inductive to deductive</cite>. <cite id="c004a74e-1">As students request information and elaborate on peers’ ideas, collective externalization and elicitation make reasoning more explicit and shared, enabling integration and conflict resolution</cite>. <cite id="c004a74e-0">Group composition and facilitation influence whether these shifts are constructive: supportive configurations and guided orchestration promote productive complementarity or reconstruction</cite>.

Mechanisms that drive process change

- Dialogic processes: externalization, elicitation, conflict resolution
  <cite id="c004a74e-1">Externalization (elaboration, agreement, answering questions) clarifies differing views and advances task-relevant knowledge; elicitation (questioning) mobilizes others’ knowledge and deepens analysis</cite>. <cite id="c004a74e-1">Acknowledging different views can lead to conflict, which must be overtaken through negotiated meanings and coordinated solutions</cite>. <cite id="c004a74e-0">Teachers can orchestrate these processes by structuring time, surfacing mathematical questions, and guiding critiques</cite>.

- Argumentative structuring: claims, evidence, warrants, and rebuttals
  <cite id="f6786a65-0">As students coordinate, claims become paired with data and articulated warrants; rebuttals specify conditions for failure and qualifiers express uncertainty</cite>. <cite id="f6786a65-1">Warrants connect evidence to claims via acceptable mathematical justifications, and critique targets the strength of this connection</cite>. <cite id="f82297c0-2">Across phases, the salience of these components shifts: warrants and data dominate in development, while socio-critical rebuttals and qualifiers gain prominence in presentation and revision</cite>.

- Role differentiation and orchestration
  <cite id="c004a74e-1">In collaborative knowledge construction, roles naturally differentiate around externalizing, eliciting, and resolving conflicts; these roles are enacted through distinct dialogic moves</cite>. <cite id="c004a74e-0">Effective facilitation ensures all members participate in critique and justification, and group composition can determine whether expertise is shared equitably</cite>. <cite id="f82297c0-0">In modeling, small-group model-building roles (defining variables, checking assumptions) and whole-group roles (interpreting, evaluating) rotate as phases progress, embedding argumentation in task roles</cite>.

Conditions that enable or hinder change

- Task affordances and composition
  <cite id="c004a74e-0">Mathematically rich tasks with multiple entry points and solution strategies support deeper reasoning and argumentation, but group composition strongly shapes discourse quality and coordination</cite>. <cite id="c004a74e-0">Heterogeneous groups can catalyze peer support and richer discussion; homogeneous groups can converge quickly but risk superficial uniformity; low-ability groups often struggle to set tasks and critique data</cite>. <cite id="f82297c0-2">Socio-critical modeling tasks further scaffold hybridization by explicitly requiring students to connect mathematical procedures to social and ethical considerations</cite>.

- Facilitation and orchestration
  <cite id="c004a74e-0">Teachers’ facilitative roles are crucial to sustain collective argumentation and to ensure that critique and public justification occur rather than premature consensus</cite>. <cite id="f6786a65-2">Instructional moves that cultivate questioning and provide knowledge of argumentation practices increase students’ opportunities to justify and convince peers, supporting social dynamics that make critique productive</cite>.

- From micro- to macro-processes
  <cite id="c004a74e-1">Micro-level dialogic moves (elaboration, agreement, questioning) accumulate into meso-level coordination (shared models, negotiated warrants), which then enable macro-level outcomes (consensus, refinement, or reconceptualization)</cite>. <cite id="c004a74e-2">At the outcome level, shifts can be complementary (expansion of one’s initial view) or reconstructive (fundamental reorganization), often accompanied by a shift from inductive to deductive reasoning as justification becomes formalized</cite>.

Illustrative trajectories

- Modeling a fair-raise task
  <cite id="f82297c0-2">In Phase 1, groups debate assumptions (e.g., counting part-time hours, defining “fair”), producing mathematical arguments to justify variable choices and calculations</cite>. <cite id="f82297c0-2">In Phase 2, whole-group presentations invite socio-critical scrutiny: students question whether the model reflects workplace ethics or equity, prompting socio-critical argumentation</cite>. <cite id="f82297c0-2">In Phase 3, returning to small groups, students integrate mathematical precision with social insight, revising models with hybrid arguments that include conditions and counterexamples to claims</cite>.

- Collaborative proof construction
  <cite id="c004a74e-2">After individual attempts, group discussion yields either complementary or reconstructive shifts in students’ arguments, with reasoning becoming deductive as warrants are articulated and critiqued</cite>. <cite id="f6786a65-0">Claims are paired with data and formal warrants; rebuttals surface edge cases, and qualifiers moderate certainty as the proof structure emerges collectively</cite>.

Practical implications for supporting change

- Design for dialogic processes
  <cite id="c004a74e-1">Provide structured prompts to elicit information (e.g., “How did you arrive at that claim?” “What data support it?”) and to acknowledge others’ ideas (e.g., “Can you elaborate on [peer]’s point?”), and explicitly plan time for conflict resolution</cite>.

- Scaffold argument structures
  <cite id="f6786a65-0">Use Toulmin-inspired graphic organizers or sentence frames (e.g., “We claim X because of Y data; the warrant is Z; a possible rebuttal is…”) to help groups externalize claims, evidence, and warrants during collaboration</cite>.

- Manage roles and equity of voice
  <cite id="c004a74e-0">Assign rotating roles (e.g., conjecturer, data-gatherer, warrant-writer, skeptic) and attend to group composition to ensure expertise sharing and sustained critique</cite>.

- Orchestrate phases and hybridization
  <cite id="f82297c0-0">Use modeling tasks that require small-group construction, whole-group critique, and revised-group implementation to make hybrid mathematical–social argumentation explicit and purposeful</cite>. <cite id="c004a74e-0">Facilitate transitions with questions that prompt justification (“Convince yourself and each other”) and critique (“What if the data were different?”)</cite>.

Residual uncertainties and contingencies
<cite id="c004a74e-0">The effectiveness of collective argumentation is contingent on composition and facilitation; patterns of success and struggle can vary across groups</cite>. <cite id="c004a74e-2">Not all students shift from inductive to deductive reasoning in groups; some maintain complementary structures, indicating that supports for formalization and critique may be necessary</cite>. <cite id="f6786a65-0">Coding shows frequent emergence of claims and data but variable development of warrants and backing; interventions that make warrants explicit may be needed to elevate quality</cite>.

Overall trajectory
As students collaborate on mathematical argumentation, their processes evolve from private sense-making and fragmented claims to coordinated, structured justifications, and then to critical evaluation and hybridization that integrate mathematical rigor with contextual and ethical considerations, with dialogic externalization, elicitation, and conflict resolution as the engines of change and with task design and facilitation as key levers. <cite id="c004a74e-1">Externalization, elicitation, and conflict resolution</cite>, <cite id="f6786a65-0">Toulmin-style structuring of claims, data, warrants, qualifiers, and rebuttals</cite>, <cite id="f82297c0-0">phase-wise shifts from model development to presentation to hybrid revision</cite>, and <cite id="c004a74e-2">individual-to-group reconceptualization and inductive-to-deductive reasoning shifts</cite> jointly describe how collaboration transforms mathematical reasoning.

Consistent with others who have documented collective mathematical practices (e.g., [5,6,32]), we used Toulmin's Model of Argumentation [33]. Briefly stated, Toulmin delineated six different aspects that comprise the structure of an everyday argument (Claim, Data, Warrant, Backing, Qualifier, and Rebuttal). Title: Emergent Collective Argumentation Types in a Socio-critical Mathematical Modeling Activity
Snippet: Socio-critical mathematical modeling encourages students to employ mathematics as a tool for social inquiry and action, promoting critical thinking and social awareness. While research on collective argumentation in mathematical modeling exists, its connection to socio-critical modeling remains underexplored. This study addresses this gap by examining the types of collective argumentation that emerge during small-group and whole-group discussions as students navigate different phases of the modeling process. Using an adapted version of Toulmin’s argumentation model and a framework for socio-critical modeling phases, this study analyzes classroom discussions in which high school students engage in a modeling task focused on fair raise distribution. The findings reveal three types of collective argumentation—mathematical, socio-critical, and hybrid— each characterized by unique aspects of student reasoning as they formulate and justify their claims. These argumentation types are linked to specific modeling process phases, illustrating dynamic interplay between student mathematical reasoning and their consideration of social and ethical issues. Our findings show that mathematical argumentation predominates in the model development phase, socio-critical argumentation in the model presentation phase, and hybrid argumentation in the model revision phase. Our work offers implications for how collective argumentation can promote equity-focused mathematical discussions in socio-critical modeling tasks.
</snippet>

Title: How Do Students' Method of Solving Proofs Change When Working in Groups?
Snippet: This study aimed to describe the shift in students’ mathematical arguments from working on a proof individually to working on it in a group. This descriptive-exploratory study used a qualitative approach. Nine undergraduate students from a private university in Jombang, Indonesia, in the 5th semester were the subjects of the study. They were selected because they had already learned the concepts of math logic, argumentation, the theory of numbers, and analysis. Hence, they were ready to construct arguments in dialogue and non-dialogue forms. A task of argumentation and an interview were used to collect data. The study had several stages. First, the students solved the given argumentation task individually. Second, they had to make small groups of 3 members and discuss the same task. The result found that four of them had a complementary shift in their arguments, while the other five students had a reconstructive shift in their views. The complementary change happened because they reconsidered their initial thoughts, complementing their previous thinking structure. On the other hand, the reconstructive shift occurred due to group discussion (i.e., dialogue), which made them reconstruct or even entirely change their previous thoughts. Furthermore, they initially used inductive reasoning and then shifted their reasoning to a deductive one.

Title: An Integrated Methodological Approach for Documenting Individual and Collective Mathematical Progress: Reinventing the Euler Method Algorithmic Tool
Snippet: Our first round of coding focused on the small group's collective mathematical progress. Consistent with others who have documented collective mathematical practices (e.g., [5,6,32]), we used Toulmin's Model of Argumentation [33]. Briefly stated, Toulmin delineated six different aspects that comprise the structure of an everyday argument (Claim, Data, Warrant, Backing, Qualifier, and Rebuttal). Numerous researchers in mathematics education have used this framework to study mathematical argumentation (e.g., [34][35][36]). However, here we use Toulmin analysis of student argumentation to document and justify our claims about the progress of students' ways of reasoning [5,24]. 

We began by coding the transcript for all Claims, Data, Warrants, Backing, Qualifiers, and Rebuttals. Claims are assertions that a speaker(s) put forth as true, and the Data are evidence to support that Claim. Typically, the Data consist of facts or procedures that lead to the conclusion that is made. A Warrant speaks to the connection between the Data and Claim. The Data-Claim-Warrant constitute the core of the argument. A Backing provides further support for the core argument. Title: Emergent Collective Argumentation Types in a Socio-critical Mathematical Modeling Activity
Snippet: Phase 1: Model Development 

In small groups, students define the problem mathematically, focusing on social problems. They make specific assumptions, identify crucial variables, and use them to construct a mathematical model to solve the problem. They prepare their solutions for a whole-group presentation. Phase 2: Model Presentation Each group presents the developed models to the whole-group, describing their approach to selecting variables and performing calculations. Groups explain their solutions, incorporating micro-level social comments (individual and personal) and macro-level social comments (broader societal perspectives) to interpret the results within the problem's context. Phase 3: Model Revision and Finalization Returning to small groups, students consider the reasonableness of their solution. They check the assumptions and mathematical procedures and determine whether they should revise their models and finalize the solutions. 

Our adaptation of Toulmin's argumentation model [67], comprising four components that guided the analysis in identifying episodes of collective argumentation during small-group and whole-group discussions, is presented in Table 2 which outlines and describes each component of collective argumentation. This adaptation offers a framework better suited to capturing each component of collective argumentation in solving a socio-critical modeling task. Counterexamples or conditions addressing potential challenges or objections to the claim.

Title: Emergent Collective Argumentation Types in a Socio-critical Mathematical Modeling Activity
Snippet: Socio-critical mathematical modeling encourages students to employ mathematics as a tool for social inquiry and action, promoting critical thinking and social awareness. While research on collective argumentation in mathematical modeling exists, its connection to socio-critical modeling remains underexplored. This study addresses this gap by examining the types of collective argumentation that emerge during small-group and whole-group discussions as students navigate different phases of the modeling process. Using an adapted version of Toulmin’s argumentation model and a framework for socio-critical modeling phases, this study analyzes classroom discussions in which high school students engage in a modeling task focused on fair raise distribution. The findings reveal three types of collective argumentation—mathematical, socio-critical, and hybrid— each characterized by unique aspects of student reasoning as they formulate and justify their claims. These argumentation types are linked to specific modeling process phases, illustrating dynamic interplay between student mathematical reasoning and their consideration of social and ethical issues. Our findings show that mathematical argumentation predominates in the model development phase, socio-critical argumentation in the model presentation phase, and hybrid argumentation in the model revision phase. Our work offers implications for how collective argumentation can promote equity-focused mathematical discussions in socio-critical modeling tasks.

Title: Emergent Collective Argumentation Types in a Socio-critical Mathematical Modeling Activity
Snippet: Three instances of mathematical argumentation addressed correcting calculation errors and revising axis titles on graphs. Four instances of socio-critical argumentation focused on assumptions concerning part-time employees' shifts and performance measures, including discussions about converting part-time positions into full-time roles instead of offering raises. During this phase, groups synthesized feedback from Phase 2's whole-group discussions to ensure their models were both mathematically sound and contextually appropriate for representing fairness in the raise distribution. The broader discussions in Phase 2, which extended ethical rights in the workplace and decisionmaking process regarding raises, set the stage for a more hybrid form of argumentation in Phase 3. This shift was driven by the need to integrate both mathematical elements and socio-critical insight that emerged during the whole-group exchange. 

Figure 5 provides a clear illustration of how collective argumentation types are linked to the modeling phases. In Phase 1, small-group discussions were dominated by mathematical arguments, while whole-group presentations emphasized socio-critical discussions. The prominence of socio-critical argumentation in Phase 2 highlights the importance of integrating broader social perspectives when justifying or sharing models with peers. Finally, the shift toward hybrid argumentation in Phase 3 underscores the integration of mathematical precision with socio-critical considerations as students refine their solutions.

Below is a synthesis of how students’ processes change as they work collaboratively on mathematical argumentation tasks, drawing on frameworks of collaborative knowledge construction, argumentation structures (Toulmin), process models of proof, and empirical classroom observations and interventions.

# Framing: Collaboration, Argumentation, and Process Change

Collaborative problem solving can motivate students to warrant their ideas and challenge others’ reasoning, thereby fostering explanations and justifications in small-group work and rich mathematical discourse when argument presentation and critique are explicitly requested and supported<cite id="4849f958-0">Solving problems together can foster students' explanations and justifications, because students become motivated to warrant their own ideas and to challenge each other's thoughts; request students to present and discuss arguments can promote rich mathematical discourse, students' use of varied reasoning and clear up some (mis)understandings</cite>. Within collaborative knowledge construction, enacted dialogue processes include externalizing task-relevant knowledge (elaborating on peers’ views, agreement moves, answering questions) and eliciting task-relevant information via questioning—moves that make views explicit, clarify misunderstandings, and integrate perspectives<cite id="4849f958-0">The framework of collaborative knowledge construction distinguishes externalization of task-relevant knowledge (elaborating on each other's views, agreement, answering questions) and request/elicitation of task-relevant information (questioning about the task), which supports using peer knowledge and clarifying prior dialogue; acknowledging different views can lead to conflict and integration</cite>.

# Phases and Trajectory: From Orientation to Integration and Consolidation

Small-group mathematical activity can be viewed as building and maintaining a shared conception of the problem, with core processes of building (introducing and accepting knowledge), monitoring ongoing activity, and repairing conflicting interpretations; as these unfold, the group transitions from initial exploration toward a coordinated understanding of the task<cite id="4849f958-4">Define collaboration as a coordinated, synchronous activity resulting from continued attempts to construct and maintain a shared conception of a problem; central activities include building by introducing and accepting knowledge, monitoring activity, and repairing conflicting interpretations</cite>. Process models of mathematical proof and argumentation emphasize iterative phases: early exploration and conjecturing followed by systematization and justification, with social-discursive argumentation needed both to refine conjectures and to synthesize into coherent arguments and proofs<cite id="920fe34c-1">Boero's process model of mathematical proof proceeds from conjecturing to proof via iterative exploratory and argumentative phases; social-discursive argumentation supports investigation, evaluation of conjectures, and synthesis of arguments and counter-arguments</cite>. In modeling contexts, small-group work often centers on model development, revision, and finalization, while whole-group debates surface and critique models; over time, data gathering, warranting, and justification become more explicit, culminating in consolidated arguments and negotiated claims<cite id="920fe34c-3">Small-group work centered on model development, revision, and finalization, whereas whole-group discussions emphasized debate; these phases prompted inductive reasoning about mathematical outcomes and social problems, with argumentation moving from exploratory to consolidated forms</cite>.

# Dialogic and Cognitive Process Changes During Collaboration

As groups progress, students’ talk shifts from orientation and exploration to integration and consolidation, with dialogic moves that scaffold reasoning quality. Early exchanges may include exploratory questions and data elicitation; as reasoning deepens, students elaborate on peers’ claims, align on definitions and procedures, and repair conflicts through argumentative moves that foreground warrants and qualifiers<cite id="4849f958-0">Dialogic processes include elaborating on others' views, agreement moves, and answering questions to influence dialogue flow; questioning about mathematics clarifies complexity and supports abstraction; processes of request/elicitation make knowledge usable as a resource</cite>. Studies of agency and collaboration show that roles change dynamically—students alternate between leading, listening, and withdrawing—and “exercised agency” (acting or refraining, contributing to the group’s joint action) becomes central to reasoning progress; productive collaboration is enacted when students build and maintain a shared conception and coordinate monitoring and repair of interpretations<cite id="4849f958-3">Roles in collaborative work change from moment to moment; agency is defined as acting or refraining and contributing to the group's joint action</cite><cite id="4849f958-4">Productive collaboration is when students build and maintain a shared conception, with processes of introducing/accepting knowledge, monitoring activity, and repairing conflicts</cite>. Empirically, groups often begin with limited justification and weak counter-argumentation, but with guidance they can develop sequences of claims, warrants, counter-claims, and synthesized rebuttals that collectively build mathematical knowledge<cite id="920fe34c-1">Students rarely justify claims and often do not take counter-arguments into account; social-discursive argumentation includes formulating structurally sound arguments and engaging in sequences of arguments, counter-arguments, and syntheses</cite><cite id="920fe34c-2">In collective argumentation, multiple students provide components of an argument; perceptions of validity can vary by person and context</cite>.

# Changes in Argumentation Structure: Claims, Warrants, and Backing

Analyzing transcripts with Toulmin’s model reveals that collaborative argumentation develops through the emergence and refinement of claims, data/evidence, warrants, backing, qualifiers, and rebuttals. Early arguments may be data-light or implicit; as groups coordinate, they increasingly articulate warrants and qualifiers and mobilize backing to address objections, thereby strengthening validity and generality<cite id="920fe34c-0">Toulmin’s model (Claim, Data, Warrant, Backing, Qualifier, Rebuttal) is used to code small-group arguments; the core Data-Claim-Warrant structure is identified, with backing, qualifiers, and rebuttals providing further support and uncertainty management; 16 arguments were identified in 10 minutes of small-group work</cite><cite id="920fe34c-2">Warrants connect data to claims; backing provides deeper support; qualifiers signal confidence; students do not always make warrants explicit, especially when warrants are perceived as implied by shared diagrams</cite>. Over time, groups move from fragmented or implicit justifications toward shared, functionally shared ways of reasoning evidenced by explicit warrants and coordinated rebuttals, indicating collective mathematical progress<cite id="920fe34c-0">We operationalized collective mathematical progress by documenting ways of reasoning that functioned-as-if-shared; emergence of these ways is evidenced by Toulmin-structured arguments within the group</cite><cite id="920fe34c-4">Explorative mathematical argumentation involves collaborative inference from premises to conclusions with reasonable justifications (data, warrants, backings) leading to construction of mathematical knowledge, with data, warrants, and claims mathematically anchored</cite>. In whole-class consolidation, collective argumentation types can be further refined and legitimated as models are critiqued and revised, elevating justification quality and social-mathematical coherence<cite id="920fe34c-3">Whole-group debates prompted students to reason inductively about outcomes and underlying problems; collective argumentation types were integrated and aligned with modeling phases, enhancing justification quality</cite>.

# Role Dynamics, Agency, and Inclusion

Process-oriented studies emphasize that students’ agency and epistemic roles change dynamically during collaboration. Students may begin as explorers or solvers, then take on roles of questioner, challenger, or synthesizer; shifts are common and contingent on the group’s needs, and sustained agency (proposing ideas, defending them, being recognized as producers) is essential for conceptual learning<cite id="4849f958-2">Mathematical reasoning is an interactional accomplishment; including all students, regardless of competence level, is central; students become producers by proposing ideas, defending them, and being recognized as such in student-student interactions</cite><cite id="4849f958-3">Roles change moment to moment; exercised agency—acting or refraining and contributing to the group’s joint action—drives reasoning progress</cite>. However, without orchestration, certain members often dominate or procedural strategies predominate; mapping role changes and ensuring equitable participation are central to sustaining high-quality argumentation and reflection at evaluation stages<cite id="4849f958-1">Group discussions have not consistently fostered meaningful mathematical argumentation; student roles tend to remain stagnant and dominated by certain individuals; limited reflection at evaluation persists</cite>. The commognitive perspective further notes that reasoning is enacted through discursive terms, routines, and visual mediators; disentangling cognitive processes from communicative practices clarifies how role changes and interaction patterns reshape reasoning quality in collaborative settings<cite id="4849f958-1">Polya’s stages and commognitive approaches show that thinking is inseparable from discursive practices; integrating them prevents mechanistic problem solving without conceptual justification</cite>.

# Teacher Orchestration and Supports: Prompting Claims, Justifications, and Critique

Teachers can prompt the development of collective argumentation by eliciting claims and justifications, encouraging critique of different arguments, modeling acceptable argument structures, and facilitating the evaluation of peers’ reasoning; these supports align with the structural (claim-justification) and dialogic (listening, building on peers, respectful critique) aspects that enable consensus-building and conceptual progress<cite id="148343d3-1">Teachers can prompt claims and justifications, encourage critical consideration of different arguments, present what constitutes acceptable mathematical arguments, and model construction and confrontation of arguments</cite><cite id="148343d3-4">Argumentation has structural aspects (building a claim with justification) and dialogic aspects (listening, building on peers’ ideas, respectful critique toward consensus); attending to both increases success in classroom argumentation</cite>. Research on noticing shows that teachers identify “critical events” in small-group argumentation—either structural (e.g., weak justification, missing warrants) or dialogic (e.g., dominance, insufficient critique)—and respond with dialogic supports (e.g., inviting warrants, redistributing talk) or cognitive feedback (e.g., pointing to reasoning quality), sometimes adopting non-intervention to allow productive struggle<cite id="148343d3-3">Teachers notice Critical Events in group argumentation (structural or dialogic, often challenges like insufficient critique or dominant students); responses draw on structural and dialogic narratives, with dialogic supports for discourse and peer critique and occasional non-intervention to foster struggle</cite>. At a broader level, intervention designs leverage transactivity—students’ active listening and building on peers’ ideas—to structure argumentation into sequences of arguments, counter-arguments, and syntheses, thereby strengthening justification and conceptual integration<cite id="920fe34c-1">Engagement in argumentation includes sequences of arguments, counter-arguments, and syntheses; computer-supported collaborative learning can develop transactive moves to strengthen argument structure</cite>.

# Representations, Models, and the Social-Warranting of Claims

In geometry and modeling tasks, students’ arguments are tightly coupled to shared diagrams, artifacts, and models; warrants may become implicit in shared visual structures, yet explicit articulation of warrants and rebuttals remains crucial to coordinate understanding and resolve disagreements<cite id="920fe34c-2">Students’ warrants and rebuttals can be inferred from diagrams; warrants are not always explicit; perceptions of validity vary by context and interlocutor</cite>. Socio-critical modeling shows how collective argumentation integrates mathematical and social dimensions, with small-group phases of model development and revision producing richer justification strategies that combine mathematical, technological, and reflexive discussions; whole-class debates then consolidate and publicize these arguments<cite id="920fe34c-3">Small-group work centers on model development and revision (emphasizing data, warrants), while whole-group debate elevates justification quality and integrates social considerations</cite>. More generally, frameworks for collective argumentation highlight steps of comparing representations, explaining/justifying them, reaching consensus, and presenting to the class—each step demanding shifts from individual reasoning to socially warranted claims<cite id="148343d3-0">Crucial steps in collective argumentation include comparing problem representations, explaining and justifying them, reaching consensus, and presenting for feedback; Toulmin-based models are widely used to identify claims, data, warrants, qualifiers, rebuttals, and backing</cite>.

# From Individual to Collective Production: What Gets Internalized and What Stays Distributed

As groups work collaboratively, the burden of justification shifts from isolated, individual productions to distributed, social warranting: claims are negotiated, data are co-collected, warrants are co-constructed and cross-checked, and rebuttals redistribute credit and authority, which supports deeper conceptual integration than individual work alone<cite id="4849f958-0">Externalization, elicitation, and conflict resolution enact collaborative knowledge construction, enabling students to clarify different views and integrate perspectives</cite><cite id="920fe34c-2">Multiple students provide components of an argument; perceptions of validity vary, underscoring distributed warranting</cite>. The notion of “functioned-as-if-shared” ways of reasoning captures how, over time, certain inferences and justifications become collectively owned even if not fully internalized by each member, evidencing progress that is both individual and group-distributed<cite id="920fe34c-0">Collective mathematical progress is evidenced by emergence of ways of reasoning that functioned-as-if-shared; Toulmin-structured arguments document these shared modes</cite>.

# Technology and Mediation: Tools for Argumentation and Monitoring

Computer-supported environments can scaffold transactive dialogue and structure argumentation phases. By making representations manipulable and histories visible, technologies support exploration of conjectures, articulation of warrants, and systematic rebuttals; studies report that such supports help students engage in sequences of argumentation and counter-argumentation that drive algebraic generalization and proof readiness<cite id="920fe34c-1">Computer-supported collaborative learning emphasizes transactivity and sequences of arguments, counter-arguments, and syntheses to strengthen justification</cite><cite id="920fe34c-2">Collective argumentation about perspective drawings shows how data, claims, and warrants are coordinated around shared diagrams; warrants may be implicit</cite>. More broadly, multi-agent discourse models (including human–companion-agent systems) illuminate how reasoning emerges through multi-voiced interactions and provide design patterns for prompts, feedback, and turn-taking that can be adapted to human groups to improve justification quality and participation equity<cite id="148343d3-0">Recent multi-agent discourse studies model collaborative mathematical activity via formal, dialectical, and argumentation-based frameworks, illuminating the multi-voiced nature of classroom reasoning</cite>.

# Practical Implications and Open Questions

- Expect early-stage collaboration to feature exploratory questions, data sharing, and tentative claims; plan for explicit instructional moves to surface warrants, qualifiers, and rebuttals as reasoning consolidates<cite id="920fe34c-0">Transcripts reveal rapid emergence of multiple arguments (claims, data, warrants) over minutes; warrants and qualifiers often underdetermine initial claims</cite><cite id="920fe34c-1">Students rarely justify claims and often neglect counter-arguments; supports are needed to elicit justification and critique</cite>.
- Design tasks and roles to cycle through conjecturing, testing, justification, critique, and consensus; use whole-group “debate” phases to refine and legitimate small-group arguments and models<cite id="920fe34c-3">Small-group development and whole-group debate align with modeling phases, elevating justification quality</cite><cite id="920fe34c-1">Balancing exploratory work with systematization and argumentation is central</cite>.
- Attend to agency: intentionally rotate leadership and challenge roles so all students exercise agency as proposer, questioner, warrant-maker, and critic; orchestrate with prompts that target both structure (“How do you know?”) and discourse (“Can you press that on Juan’s idea?”)<cite id="4849f958-2">Students become producers by proposing and defending ideas and being recognized as such in student-student interactions</cite><cite id="148343d3-1">Teachers can prompt claims and justifications, encourage critique, and model acceptable arguments</cite>.
- Monitor for dialogic and structural “critical events” and respond with targeted supports (e.g., inviting warrants, redistributing talk, inviting rebuttals), sometimes withholding to preserve productive struggle<cite id="148343d3-3">Teachers notice structural/dialogic challenges and respond with dialogic supports, cognitive feedback, or non-intervention to enable struggle</cite>.

In sum, collaborative mathematical argumentation reshapes individual processes from exploratory conjecturing and isolated reasoning toward distributed, socially warranted claims: students externalize and elaborate ideas, elicit and question evidence, coordinate monitoring and repair, and progressively articulate claims, data, warrants, qualifiers, and rebuttals that collectively integrate and consolidate mathematical understanding<cite id="4849f958-0">Collaborative knowledge construction enacts externalization and elicitation through dialogic moves that clarify and integrate views</cite><cite id="920fe34c-0">Toulmin-structured arguments emerge over time and document collective mathematical progress</cite><cite id="920fe34c-4">Explorative argumentation leads to construction of knowledge via anchored data, warrants, and claims</cite>. Teacher orchestration and technological mediation can catalyze these shifts by structuring transactive dialogue, surfacing warrants, and equalizing participation, thereby transforming raw collaborative talk into coherent, collectively owned mathematical arguments<cite id="920fe34c-1">Transactivity and structured argumentation sequences strengthen justification and synthesis</cite><cite id="148343d3-1">Teacher prompts and modeling support claims, justifications, critique, and consensus</cite>.

Title: An Integrated Methodological Approach for Documenting Individual and Collective Mathematical Progress: Reinventing the Euler Method Algorithmic Tool
Snippet: Our first round of coding focused on the small group's collective mathematical progress. Consistent with others who have documented collective mathematical practices (e.g., [5,6,32]), we used Toulmin's Model of Argumentation [33]. Briefly stated, Toulmin delineated six different aspects that comprise the structure of an everyday argument (Claim, Data, Warrant, Backing, Qualifier, and Rebuttal). Numerous researchers in mathematics education have used this framework to study mathematical argumentation (e.g., [34][35][36]). However, here we use Toulmin analysis of student argumentation to document and justify our claims about the progress of students' ways of reasoning [5,24]. 

We began by coding the transcript for all Claims, Data, Warrants, Backing, Qualifiers, and Rebuttals. Claims are assertions that a speaker(s) put forth as true, and the Data are evidence to support that Claim. Typically, the Data consist of facts or procedures that lead to the conclusion that is made. A Warrant speaks to the connection between the Data and Claim. The Data-Claim-Warrant constitute the core of the argument. A Backing provides further support for the core argument. A Qualifier speaks to the degree or level of confidence in the Claim, and a Rebuttal is an objection that offers conditions under which the Claim is invalid. In order to count as an argument, we required there to be at least a Data-Claim pair (i.e., Claims with no supporting justification were not counted as arguments). In total, we identified 16 different arguments in the 10 min small group work. The majority of these are detailed in the next main section. 

Next, we operationalized the small group's collective mathematical progress by documenting mathematical ways of reasoning that functioned-as-if-shared for this small group. In this case, the collective mathematical progress is evidenced by the emergence of ways of reasoning that function-as-if-shared. To document collective mathematical practices, we used of the methodology detailed in [19] (we refer readers to this chapter for details on the method).

Title: Developing argumentation skills in mathematics through computer-supported collaborative learning: the role of transactivity
Snippet: Argumentation skills are required for individuals to be able to participate in apparently open-ended discussions not only in political and philosophical domains, but also in domains that are usually more driven by formal rules and deductive approaches such as mathematics. An engagement in meaningful activities like mathematical argumentation and proof is increasingly postulated as a goal of mathematical education (National Council of Teachers of Mathematics 2000). Boero (1999) proposed a process model of mathematical proof that starts from finding a conjecture and proceeds to the final formulation of a proof through phases of exploration as well as phases of systematization. This model includes iterative steps of balancing informal explorations and corresponding mathematical arguments that can collaboratively be discussed with others (Reiss et al. 2008). The discussion with others is considered a promising way to strengthen the approach to solving the proof task, since others may bring in new ideas and perspectives to refine original ideas and arguments. 

Thus, social-discursive argumentation skills are required at different points either to construct sound arguments (Pease et al. 2009) or to be able to engage in an argumentative dialogue, as mathematicians indeed ''prove things in a social context and address them to a certain audience'' (Thurston 1994, p. 175). For instance, social-discursive argumentation can already be an important part in Boero's (1999) first step, which includes investigation of the problem space to come up with a reasonable conjecture. Within this step, two learners might investigate different parts of the problem space (e.g., negative and positive numbers) by different methods and come up with different conjectures. Then the learners need to discuss how reasonable the different conjectures are and which conjecture should further be followed to prove it. In this article, we focus on this social-discursive component of argumentation skills, which includes the skills to formulate structurally sound arguments (Toulmin 1958) and to engage in argumentative discourse with a learning partner, consisting of sequences of arguments, counter-arguments, and syntheses (Leita ˜o 2000). 

Yet, engaging in meaningful argumentation is challenging for students. As prior research has shown, they rarely justify claims and often do not take counter-arguments into account (Sadler 2004).
</snippet>

Title: Geometry Students’ Arguments About a 1-Point Perspective Drawing
Snippet: We assume the perspective that learning is participation in a community of practice, in this case the classroom (Lave & Wenger, 1991). An integral aspect of students' learning in mathematics classrooms is participating in mathematical discussions (Forman, Larreamendy-Joerns, Stein, & Brown, 1998;Forman, McCormick, & Donato, 1997;Moschkovich, 2012;Zahner, 2012). Recent policy documents emphasize that students should have opportunities to formulate arguments and critique the reasoning of their peers (NGAC, 2010;NCTM, 2000). This practice is supported by research suggesting that devising and refining arguments can support mathematical understanding (Jahnke, 2008;Stephan & Akyuz, 2012;Yackel, 2002). Because of the value of mathematical argumentation, and the difficulty of it in a small group setting, there is opportunity to better understand how students work together to build mathematical arguments. 

We use Toulmin's (1958) model of an argument to examine how students working together in groups built arguments about a 1-point perspective drawing. There are six components to an argument: the data or evidence on which the argument is based; the claim of the argument; the warrant, or justification for the claim based on the data; a backing, or underlying rationale for the warrant; a rebuttal which offers a contradiction to the claim; and a qualifier that communicates the strength of the claim. Students do not always make the warrants of their claims explicit, in particular when they perceive the warrant may be implied through a shared diagram (Hollebrands et al., 2010). Particularly important for this study, the ways that students warrant their claims or offer rebuttals to others' arguments can indicate the sources of prior knowledge they draw upon to formulate those arguments. 

In collective argumentation, multiple students provide the components of an argument (Forman et al., 1998;Moore-Russo et al., 2011;Yackel, 2002). Whether or not students perceive one another's justifications as valid can vary according to the person and context (Forman et al., 1998;Krummheuer, 1995).

Title: Emergent Collective Argumentation Types in a Socio-critical Mathematical Modeling Activity
Snippet: Argumentation refers to constructing, presenting, and evaluating arguments to justify a position or persuade others [51]. Argumentation can be individual or collective [38]. Individual argumentation might aim to convince an audience about the validity of a claim, whereas collective argumentation strives to build a shared understanding where a group of individuals collaborate to establish a claim and persuade others [56]. Demiray and collaborators [20] identified crucial steps in collective argumentation: comparing problem representations in a small group, explaining and justifying these representations, reaching a group consensus, and presenting their ideas to the class for feedback from peers and the teacher. 

Research on collective argumentation has significantly increased, exploring aspects of mathematics teaching and learning to enhance student reasoning and learning [18,45]. Moreover, research has assessed improving academic performance and self-efficacy [39,64] and examining the role of teacher knowledge and practices in supporting this process [12,16,17,24,36,43]. 

Recent work on multi-agent discourse further broadens this perspective by examining how mathematical reasoning and argumentation emerge through interactions among human and computational agents. Studies in this line have modeled collaborative mathematical activity through formal, dialectical, and argumentation-based frameworks that illuminate the dynamic, multi-voiced nature of reasoning in education and beyond [4,44,50]. 

Toulmin's argumentation model [67] has commonly been applied to identify arguments in small-group or class discussions [6,18,66,35,40]. The model outlines arguments via six components: claim (a statement), data (facts supporting the claim), warrant (justification for using the data to establish the claim), qualifier (indicating the certainty of a statement), rebuttal (statements that question the warrant), and backing (support for the warrant). Krummheuer [37] introduced a simplified version of this model. Despite its limitations [32], the core components-claim, data, and warrant-were deemed sufficient to analyze collective argumentation [34]. Studies have since adopted Krummheuer's simplified model (e.g., [24]) or modified Toulmin's argumentation model (e.g., [46]) to dissect and evaluate collective argumentation components.
</snippet>

Title: Supporting argumentation in mathematics classrooms
Snippet: When supporting students working collaboratively to develop mathematical arguments, teachers can prompt students to establish claims and justifications, encourage them to critically consider different arguments, present to students what constitutes acceptable mathematical arguments, and model ways of constructing and confronting arguments (Ayalon & Hershkowitz, 2017). 

Despite its importance for mathematical learning, the implementation of argumentation in mathematics classrooms is not common practice (Bieda, 2010;Bleiler, Thompson, & Krajcevski, 2014;Staples, Bartlo, & Thanheiser, 2012). Research shows that teachers find it challenging to incorporate this practice in classrooms (Ayalon & Even, 2016;Bieda, 2010). They find it challenging to engage students in constructing and critiquing arguments (e.g., Ayalon & Even, 2016) and their interpretations of facilitating argumentation may not be aligned with those of reformers such as assuming that mathematical argumentation can occur with relatively little scaffolding by the teacher (Kosko et al., 2014). There is a general consensus that research on teacher support of argumentation is still in its infancy and more needs to be known about teacher knowledge and practice of argumentation (Kosko et al., 2014;Mueller et al., 2014). This study addresses this issue by examining aspects of mathematical knowledge that influence teacher's support of argumentation.

Snippet: Argumentation is the process by which individuals construct and critique arguments; 

an argument is the product of argumentation (Nussbaum, 2011). In this study, we use the term collective argumentation when teachers or students make claims and provide evidence and reasoning to support them in a social setting (Conner et al., 2014; see also Forman et al., 1998;Krummheuer, 1995;Whitenack & Knipping, 2002;Yackel, 2002). Other researchers have similarly described our sense of collective argumentation as collaborative argumentation (Nussbaum, 2008), critical discussions (Keefer et al, 2000), accountable talk (Michaels et al., 2008), and exploratory talk (Mercer, 2000). Collective argumentation and these other similar classroombased discussions have been found to promote students' conceptual understanding of content (Kim & Hand, 2015;Nussbaum, 2008;Walshaw & Anthony, 2008;Webb et al., 2019). 

Toulmin's Model for Argumentation Toulmin's (1958Toulmin's ( /2003) ) model for argumentation has been a prominent theoretical framework for education researchers studying the content and structure of argumentation (Nussbaum, 2011). 

Many mathematics and science education scholars have applied Toulmin's model to analyze argumentation practices in classrooms (e.g., Cross, 2009;Erduran et al., 2004;Krummheuer, 1995;Osborne et al., 2004;Yackel, 2002;Zohar & Nemet, 2002). We follow Krummheuer's (1995) adaptation of Toulmin's model and the work of other mathematics education researchers building on Krummheuer's work (e.g., Forman et al., 1998;Knipping, 2008;Rasmussen et al., 2015;Yackel, 2002). 

The core structure of Toulmin's model includes a statement that is being established (i.e., claim) with evidence to support the statement (i.e., data), and reasoning justifying the relation of the evidence for supporting the statement (i.e., warrant).

Title: Mathematics teachers’ noticing of argumentation within small groups
Snippet: This study examined how secondary-school mathematics teachers notice Critical Events associated with Group Mathematical Argumentation (CEGMAs), focusing on attending, interpreting, and responding. We interpret the findings through cognitive and socio-cultural lenses, highlighting professional narratives that shape teachers' reasoning. 

We then discuss the study's theoretical and practical contributions, limitations, and directions for future research. 

In relation to the first research question: What characterizes the CEGMAs identified by teachers? Participants identified events with either a structural or dialogic focus, with a few combining both. These choices reflect different facets of small-group argumentation and were often oriented toward challenges (e.g., insufficient critique, dominant students), echoing prior findings that teachers more readily identify difficulties than successes (Scheiner, 2023). The wording of the task prompt-asking teachers to identify "moments with potential for argumentation to develop"-may have contributed to this pattern, by steering attention toward difficulties or challenges as potential starting points for argumentation rather than to moments of successful engagement. This suggests that future studies explore how different prompts shape what teachers attend to and how they frame their pedagogical role. 

Addressing the second research question: How do teachers interpret the CEGMAs they chose, and what types of responses do they propose? We found that teachers' interpretive and responsive reasoning was guided by professional narratives that varied in both structural/ dialogic aspects and cognitive, social, and affective dimensions. These narratives functioned as interpretive lenses through which teachers made sense of students' argumentation and justified their proposed responses (Goodwin, 1994). The prominence of cognitive dimensions, especially in structural narratives, suggests that teachers often framed argumentation events in terms of reasoning, conceptual understanding, or justification. At the same time, dialogic narratives were particularly salient in teachers' proposed responses, highlighting support for group discourse and peer critique. Importantly, even rare cases of deliberate non-intervention point to a more nuanced pedagogical stance, where teachers recognized that meaningful argumentation may unfold without direct input. Such stances echo the notion of productive struggle, where withholding intervention can foster deeper engagement (Kapur, 2014).
</snippet>

The theoretical perspective for the approach taken in this paper views argumentation as a social process, situated, in our case, in the social norms of the classroom. We therefore follow van Eemeren's and Grootendorst's (2004) definition according to which argumentation is "a verbal, social, and rational activity aimed at convincing a reasonable critic of the acceptability of a standpoint by putting forward a constellation of propositions justifying or refuting the proposition expressed in the standpoint" (p 1). This definition posits argumentation in a social space and lays the groundwork for common descriptions of "deliberative argumentation" which have been shown to be notably 'fruitful' for learning (Felton et al. 2009). Learners' collaborative construction of arguments, listening critically yet respectfully to their peers' ideas, identifying the advantages and drawbacks in each idea, and striving toward a general consensus are the key features of this form of argumentation, according to Asterhan and Schwarz (2016, p 167). 

Following González-Howard and McNeill (2020), in this study we consider argumentation as having two prominent and interrelated aspects: (1) the structural aspects, which consist of building a claim and suggesting an appropriate justification for it and (2) the dialogic aspects, which focus on individuals' interactions when listening to one another, building upon their peers' proposed ideas, and respectfully critiquing those ideas as the group works together toward attaining a consensus. In our opinion, teachers will attain greater success in incorporating argumentation into their classrooms by attending to both aspects of argumentation.

# Framing: Collaboration, Argumentation, and Process Change

Collaborative problem solving can motivate students to warrant their ideas and challenge others’ reasoning, thereby fostering explanations and justifications in small-group work and rich mathematical discourse when argument presentation and critique are explicitly requested and supported<cite id="4849f958-0">Solving problems together can foster students' explanations and justifications, because students become motivated to warrant their own ideas and to challenge each other's thoughts; request students to present and discuss arguments can promote rich mathematical discourse, students' use of varied reasoning and clear up some (mis)understandings</cite>. # Phases and Trajectory: From Orientation to Integration and Consolidation

Small-group mathematical activity can be viewed as building and maintaining a shared conception of the problem, with core processes of building (introducing and accepting knowledge), monitoring ongoing activity, and repairing conflicting interpretations; as these unfold, the group transitions from initial exploration toward a coordinated understanding of the task<cite id="4849f958-4">Define collaboration as a coordinated, synchronous activity resulting from continued attempts to construct and maintain a shared conception of a problem; central activities include building by introducing and accepting knowledge, monitoring activity, and repairing conflicting interpretations</cite>. Process models of mathematical proof and argumentation emphasize iterative phases: early exploration and conjecturing followed by systematization and justification, with social-discursive argumentation needed both to refine conjectures and to synthesize into coherent arguments and proofs<cite id="920fe34c-1">Boero's process model of mathematical proof proceeds from conjecturing to proof via iterative exploratory and argumentative phases; social-discursive argumentation supports investigation, evaluation of conjectures, and synthesis of arguments and counter-arguments</cite>. In modeling contexts, small-group work often centers on model development, revision, and finalization, while whole-group debates surface and critique models; over time, data gathering, warranting, and justification become more explicit, culminating in consolidated arguments and negotiated claims<cite id="920fe34c-3">Small-group work centered on model development, revision, and finalization, whereas whole-group discussions emphasized debate; these phases prompted inductive reasoning about mathematical outcomes and social problems, with argumentation moving from exploratory to consolidated forms</cite>.

# Dialogic and Cognitive Process Changes During Collaboration

As groups progress, students’ talk shifts from orientation and exploration to integration and consolidation, with dialogic moves that scaffold reasoning quality. Early exchanges may include exploratory questions and data elicitation; as reasoning deepens, students elaborate on peers’ claims, align on definitions and procedures, and repair conflicts through argumentative moves that foreground warrants and qualifiers<cite id="4849f958-0">Dialogic processes include elaborating on others' views, agreement moves, and answering questions to influence dialogue flow; questioning about mathematics clarifies complexity and supports abstraction; processes of request/elicitation make knowledge usable as a resource</cite>. Studies of agency and collaboration show that roles change dynamically—students alternate between leading, listening, and withdrawing—and “exercised agency” (acting or refraining, contributing to the group’s joint action) becomes central to reasoning progress; productive collaboration is enacted when students build and maintain a shared conception and coordinate monitoring and repair of interpretations<cite id="4849f958-3">Roles in collaborative work change from moment to moment; agency is defined as acting or refraining and contributing to the group's joint action</cite><cite id="4849f958-4">Productive collaboration is when students build and maintain a shared conception, with processes of introducing/accepting knowledge, monitoring activity, and repairing conflicts</cite>. # Changes in Argumentation Structure: Claims, Warrants, and Backing

Analyzing transcripts with Toulmin’s model reveals that collaborative argumentation develops through the emergence and refinement of claims, data/evidence, warrants, backing, qualifiers, and rebuttals. # Role Dynamics, Agency, and Inclusion

Process-oriented studies emphasize that students’ agency and epistemic roles change dynamically during collaboration. Students may begin as explorers or solvers, then take on roles of questioner, challenger, or synthesizer; shifts are common and contingent on the group’s needs, and sustained agency (proposing ideas, defending them, being recognized as producers) is essential for conceptual learning<cite id="4849f958-2">Mathematical reasoning is an interactional accomplishment; including all students, regardless of competence level, is central; students become producers by proposing ideas, defending them, and being recognized as such in student-student interactions</cite><cite id="4849f958-3">Roles change moment to moment; exercised agency—acting or refraining and contributing to the group’s joint action—drives reasoning progress</cite>. # Teacher Orchestration and Supports: Prompting Claims, Justifications, and Critique

Teachers can prompt the development of collective argumentation by eliciting claims and justifications, encouraging critique of different arguments, modeling acceptable argument structures, and facilitating the evaluation of peers’ reasoning; these supports align with the structural (claim-justification) and dialogic (listening, building on peers, respectful critique) aspects that enable consensus-building and conceptual progress<cite id="148343d3-1">Teachers can prompt claims and justifications, encourage critical consideration of different arguments, present what constitutes acceptable mathematical arguments, and model construction and confrontation of arguments</cite><cite id="148343d3-4">Argumentation has structural aspects (building a claim with justification) and dialogic aspects (listening, building on peers’ ideas, respectful critique toward consensus); attending to both increases success in classroom argumentation</cite>. # From Individual to Collective Production: What Gets Internalized and What Stays Distributed

As groups work collaboratively, the burden of justification shifts from isolated, individual productions to distributed, social warranting: claims are negotiated, data are co-collected, warrants are co-constructed and cross-checked, and rebuttals redistribute credit and authority, which supports deeper conceptual integration than individual work alone<cite id="4849f958-0">Externalization, elicitation, and conflict resolution enact collaborative knowledge construction, enabling students to clarify different views and integrate perspectives</cite><cite id="920fe34c-2">Multiple students provide components of an argument; perceptions of validity vary, underscoring distributed warranting</cite>. # Technology and Mediation: Tools for Argumentation and Monitoring

Title: Exploring Polya's Problem-Solving Stages, Cognitive Components, and Role Change Dynamics in Mathematical Problem-Solving Discussions
Snippet: The background of this research lies in the conceptual and empirical gap between the success of procedural mathematical problem solving and the quality of the thinking process and accompanying discourse in collaborative learning. Various studies show that problem-solving learning is still predominantly assessed by final results. At the same time, the dynamics of thinking, the negotiation of meaning, and changes in students' epistemic roles in discussions have not been systematically mapped (Fabiani Marcatto, 2025;Oktaviani et al., 2020;Wiyah & Nurjanah, 2021). Polya's problem-solving stages have long been recognized as a fundamental heuristic framework, but their implementation is often decoupled from the analysis of mathematical communication in group discussions. On the other hand, the commognitive approach asserts that mathematical thinking cannot be separated from discursive practices involving terms, routines, and visual mediators (Barnett, 2022;Lu et al., 2023;Martín Molina et al., 2020). When these two frameworks are not explicitly integrated, learning risks producing mechanistic problem-solving without a strong conceptual justification. The urgency of this research is further heightened because problem-solving discussions are central to modern collaborative mathematics learning, where changes in participants' roles directly affect the quality of mathematical reasoning and decision-making (Felmer, 2023;Muslim et al., 2024). 

Empirical evidence from international, national, and local studies collectively indicates that mathematical problem-solving skills face serious and persistent challenges. Cross-country reports show that students frequently struggle with planning and evaluating solutions, even when basic procedural execution is manageable (Iilonga & Ogbonnaya, 2023;S. Zhang et al., 2022). National and regional studies reveal that group discussions have not consistently fostered meaningful mathematical argumentation, as student roles tend to remain stagnant and dominated by certain individuals (Fatmanissa et al., 2022;Gustafsson, 2024;Sutama et al., 2022). Studies in teacher education contexts also indicate the dominance of procedural strategies and limited reflection at the evaluation stage, resulting in restricted mathematical argumentation during discussions (Lathifaturrahmah et al., 2024;Wiyah & Nurjanah, 2021).

Title: Students’ agency, creative reasoning, and collaboration in mathematical problem solving
Snippet: Opportunities for studying situations of collaborative processes are in this study viewed through a problem-solving session, emphasizing active engagement in a learning process (Lithner, 2017). An active learning process is not common in so-called easier learning processes where solution procedures are imitated but rather found in students' problem solving when they attempt to construct their own solution procedures through reasoning (Lithner, 2017). Mathematical reasoning is a central interactional aspect of learning mathematics where arguments are important for the learning process and not only as an outcome of learning mathematics (Yackel, 2001). Therefore, this study views mathematical argumentation and reasoning as an interactional accomplishment and what students "take as acceptable, individually and collectively, and not whether an argument might be considered mathematically valid" (Yackel, 2001, p. 6). In line with this view, including all students at any competence level in mathematics, is Lithner's framework of mathematical reasoning (Lithner, 2008(Lithner, , 2017)). From this framework, a student's reasoning is explained as "the line of thought adopted to produce assertions and reach conclusions in task solving" (Lithner, 2017, p. 939). 

In situations of mathematical communication, a student may become a producer of mathematics through their own and joint processes of grappling and exploring mathematics, sometimes hitting the wrong trail, and sometimes making sense of solutions, rather than being a reproducer (Freudenthal, 1991;Schoenfeld, 2013). Schoenfeld (2013) says: "A major issue is, when if ever do students get to develop a mathematical voice? That is, when do they get to propose ideas and answers, defend them, and become recognized as producers of mathematics themselves?" (p. 613). If these situations of mathematical communication include mathematical talk between students, they are in a student-student interaction. How well students interact in pairs and small groups is important for students' progress in becoming a mathematical producer, rather than an imitator who reproduces mathematics without understanding the conceptual parts (Lithner, 2017). Varhol et al. (2020) researched student interactions and found that some specific types of interactions were important for making mathematical progress in algebraic generalization.

Title: Students’ agency, creative reasoning, and collaboration in mathematical problem solving

That study, and other studies on students' group work or pairwise collaboration, contends that quality student interactions and the dynamics of the processes in students' collaborations need to be further explored (Seidouvy & Schindler, 2019;van de Pol et al., 2018;Varhol et al., 2020). 

Students engage with one another and take on different roles while interacting. Sometimes a student leads the conversation, other times he or she might listen or withdraw from the conversation. Thus, roles in collaborative work can "change from moment to moment" (Child & Shaw, 2018, p. 1). Hence, another central interactional aspect in group work, when considering students' actions and engagement in reasoning and collaboration, is students' exercised agency (Mueller et al., 2012). This study see agency as Gresalfi et al. (2009) define it; "the way in which he or she acts, or refrains from acting, and the way in which her or his action contributes to the joint action of the group in which he or she is participating" (p. 53). 

The field needs a better understanding of peer interaction patterns in collaborative mathematical activity. Little is known about the dynamics of students' collaborative interaction in mathematics classroom, and few studies have taken the process view of collaboration (Seidouvy & Schindler, 2019). This study focuses on three particular aspects of students' interactions: collaborative processes, mathematical reasoning, and exercised agency. To investigate conditions for fruitful collaboration, Kuhn (2015) states that "it is essential to understand the underlying mechanisms" (p. 47). Studying interactional aspects separately and seen in interplay in students' interaction patterns may therefore give a better understanding of underlying processes of collaboration, which can furthermore enable collaborative aspects to become teachable. Research on collaboration (Child & Shaw, 2018;Kuhn, 2015) and reasoning (Lithner, 2017) argues that learning is enacted in both instances and that there is a need for insights of the underlying processes causing this learning opportunity.

documents.snippet:
Students' mathematical communication, reasoning, and problem-solving are highlighted in the research literature as important aspects for fostering students' learning of mathematics (Pijls & Dekker, 2011;Seidouvy & Schindler, 2019;Sidenvall, 2019). Therefore, promoting students' mathematical communication such as making reasoning meaningful to oneself and peers, listening to one another, and solving mathematics together (Mueller et al., 2012) are central issues for progress in their mathematical understanding. Students' collaboration and reasoning are key interactional aspects in math-talk and small group work. It is a well-researched area but still highlighted as a topic where more knowledge is needed, because when students are given the opportunity they can construct their own solution procedures, important for their mathematical understanding (cf., Lithner, 2017;Mueller et al., 2012;Stockero et al., 2019). 

Collaboration in classrooms has often been studied as an outcome or as a process (Dillenbourg et al., 1996). A research approach on the outcome is often seen as an individual's activity with focus on learning (Child & Shaw, 2018;Dillenbourg et al., 1996), whereas a research approach on collaborative processes emphasize the whole group and in particular the participant interaction (Seidouvy and Schindler, 2019). With the latter view on collaboration, this study defines collaboration as "a coordinated, synchronous activity that is the result of a continued attempt to construct and maintain a shared conception of a problem" (Roschelle & Teasley, 1995, p. 70). With this focus, the study views productive collaboration enacted when students build and maintain a shared conception of a mathematical problem, which is their shared understanding of the problem at hand (Roschelle & Teasley, 1995). Moreover, for students to pool their knowledge together for a shared understanding, the study sees the processes of building by introducing and accepting knowledge, monitoring ongoing activity, and repairing conflicting interpretations, as central activities for such interaction. 

Opportunities for studying situations of collaborative processes are in this study viewed through a problem-solving session, emphasizing active engagement in a learning process (Lithner, 2017).
